translations.t_ayuda_patrones:
Patterns in URLs

  *        anything within one segment (does not cross «/»)
  ?        one character
  [abc]    one of those; [a-z] a range; [!x] anything but x
  {a,b*}   alternatives, each with its own wildcards; spaces allowed

They work in any segment: connection, pool, dataset, @snapshot and the
detail of #properties, #content and #path. Case-sensitive, like ZFS.
A literal wildcard is written encoded: %2A is a real «*».

In «ls», the last segment FILTERS what is listed:
  ls tank/user/M*                  children of tank/user starting with M
  ls tank/data@auto-2024-*         only those snapshots
  ls tank#properties/{a*, b*}      properties starting with a or b
  ls zfsm://{fc16,unib}/*          the pools of both machines

In reads —get, info, status, history…— every matching target is handled,
and their tables are joined into one with a TARGET column.

In those that MODIFY —destroy, set, mount, unmount, hold, release,
scrub, install-daemon— the pattern may only be in the last segment, the
exact list is ALWAYS shown, and confirmation is asked unless -y. With
--check you see the list without touching anything:
  destroy tank/data@auto-2024-* --check

Copying, as in the shell: the SOURCE may match several and the target
only one.
  cp tank#content/*.log unib/sback        the .log files, each with its name
  cp /var/log/*.log tank                  also from a local path
  rsync tank/copy --from tank#content/s*  copy/s1, copy/s2…, as in rsync
Two sources that would land with the same name are rejected, and «*» does
not pick hidden files. Without wildcards, «#content/{a,b}» in rsync puts
the content of each into the target, as always.

«cd», «send» and «diff» accept a pattern if it matches exactly one.
Commands that act on one by definition —rename, rollback, create,
clone…— reject it.
If nothing matches it is an error; the pattern is never passed as is.
translations.t_ayuda_urls:
How each thing is named

  zfsm://                          the root: the connections
  zfsm://host                      a machine
  zfsm://host/tank/data            a pool or a dataset
  zfsm://host/tank/data@yesterday  a snapshot
  zfsm://host/tank/data#content/a  a file or directory OF the dataset
  zfsm://host#path/var/log         any path of the machine
  zfsm://w11#path/C:/Users         on Windows, the drive goes first

#path hangs from the machine, never from a dataset: inside a dataset it is
#content. EVERY command understands it; what changes is what each one can
do with it:

  ls, cd, info, cp, rsync      the path is what they handle
  todir, fromdir, labelclear,  the path instead of a bare «/path»; the URL
  import -d, pool disks        also says on which machine
  dataset and pool commands    ONLY if the path is exactly the mountpoint
                               (or .zfs/snapshot/<s>); what it stands for
                               is shown before acting

Being INSIDE a dataset is not enough, and it never climbs to the one holding it:
  destroy zfsm://m#path/mnt/tank/data/photos
  → is not a dataset; it is inside tank/data:
    zfsm://m/tank/data#content/photos
To delete THAT file or directory: «destroy [-r] …#content/photos».

Inside #content or #path, «cd sub» and «cd ..» move through directories,
and tab offers the names in each one.

An UNMOUNTED dataset can be looked at too: #content mounts it read-only on a
temporary directory, without changing its mountpoint, and releases it when you
leave it. Nothing is mounted for writing: that is «mount». Not on Windows
nor on macOS, whose mount_zfs does not honour read-only.

translations.t_bd_det1: The arguments go in PAIRS: each subdirectory with the name of the dataset that replaces it. From the outside nothing moves: where there was a directory there is now a dataset with the same contents, and with its own properties, snapshots and quota.
translations.t_bd_det2: The name does NOT have to mirror the path: creating a dataset only requires its parent to exist by name, so `breakdown a/b/c a:b:c` converts the three-level one without converting `a` or `b`.
translations.t_bd_det3: Every byte moves ONCE and the originals are deleted at the end, once every copy is verified: if something fails midway, the original is still intact. That is why it is worth leaving it as a JOB —without --wait— when there is volume: follow it with «job <id>» and the interpreter stays free.

translations.t_sch_det3: The one taking the snapshots is that machine's GSA agent, not this program: if it is not installed, the schedule is written and nothing happens. translations.t_sch_det4: «schedule status» tells what happened in the last pass of each schedule: the snapshot, the pruning, the levelling and the pruning of the target, and if something failed, when and why. The levelling goes apart, as a JOB of the daemon: it shows in «jobs», is followed with «job <id>» and stopped with «job cancel <id>». With «--wait», it waits here for it to finish. A cancelled levelling is not retried by itself: it waits for the next snapshot or another «schedule run».
translations.t_sch_det6: Levelling leaves the target with the same snapshots as the source: it sends with «zfs send -I» from the newest common one —found by guid—, and prunes on the target the scheduled snapshots the source no longer has. translations.t_sch_det7: If the dataset has not changed since the newest snapshot of a class, no new one is taken: that one is renamed to the new name, so the retention does not spend a slot on something that adds nothing. With atime=on, reading files already counts as a change.
translations.t_sch_det8: Pruning never destroys the base of the levelling, even when it falls outside the retention: so with the target down for a few days, it catches up by itself when it comes back.

translations.t_uso_s_opci_010447:
Usage: %s [options] <command>

With no command it enters INTERACTIVE MODE: a shell where the location
is a zfsm:// URL and every command acts on it.

Commands:
  (none)                Interactive mode, starting at zfsm://Local
  connections list      Lists the configured connections
  url parse <zfsm://…>  Parses a URL and shows what it names
  version               This tool's version

Options:
  --password-fd <n>     Read the master password from that descriptor.
                        Without it, it is asked for on the terminal.
  --config-dir <path>   Configuration directory (by default,
                        ~/.config/ZFSMgr)
  --no-secrets          Decrypts nothing: does not ask for a master password.
                        Encrypted fields come out as <cifrado>.
  --format text|tsv|json
                        text (the default) is for reading; tsv is for
                        scripts: no header, tabs, fixed columns
                        in English and «-» where there is no value, just
                        like `zfs list -H`; json is for programs:
                        numbers come out as numbers, booleans as
                        booleans and what does not apply as null.
                        connections list: id, name, type, os, user,
                        host, port, sudo, tls, connected
  --url <zfsm://…>      Where to start in interactive mode
  --lang es|en          Language of the messages. Without it, the one the
                        GUI uses (app.language in config.json).
  -v, --verbose         Reports on standard error what the transport
                        does with each machine
  -y, --yes             Do not ask before destructive actions
  --no-schedule-check   Do not check the state of the snapshot schedules
                        when starting
  --no-tui              Plain terminal: no multi-line editing, no redraw
                        on resize and no status area
  -h, --help            This help

The master password is NOT passed as an argument or an environment
variable: both are visible in `ps` to any user of the machine. With the
descriptor any secret manager can be used:

  %s --password-fd 3 connections list  3< <(pass show zfsmgr)
